headline: Child-safety advocates say regulators should act on AI risks for children sooner than they did on social media, the Associated Press reports.
score_reason: Kept at 5: AP analysis with named experts and Pew data; no new development.
importance_line: Children and parents face new chatbot risks while rules lag, which matters first to families and teenagers (64% of US teens have used chatbots, per Pew), then to lawmakers, but the article reports no new evidence of harm and the bills are at an early stage.
summary: The Associated Press reports that parent advocates and researchers want lessons from social media's child-safety fight, including this summer's $18 billion settlement in which Meta agreed to safeguards, applied to AI sooner, and that AI firms have so far moved somewhat faster than social media firms did. OpenAI added teen accounts in August, about four years after launching ChatGPT, but experts say Meta's protections cannot simply be copied because teenagers also use chatbots for homework, and child-safety AI bills have cleared Senate subcommittees but face a long road while states move faster.
notes: Original on apnews.com returned 403; text read in the Republican Herald's copy of the AP story (by Kaitlyn Huamani and Barbara Ortutay). Credit goes to the Associated Press, the original reporter; url is the AP original.
